job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Meridian Ocean Minerals. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Meridian Ocean Minerals is a deep-sea mining company headquartered in Houston, with a policy office in Washington, DC. Our mission is to commercially recover polymetallic nodules from the deep seabed, a vast source of nickel, cobalt, manganese, and copper, and to supply these critical minerals for batteries, the energy transition, and economic growth. We believe the United States must lead in this industry. Our policy team works with lawmakers to protect our ability to continue exploration and commercial development.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which would shut down our core work and which we strongly oppose. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
**S. 2817 — Loopholes, Ambiguities, and Drafting Problems**

**Definitions (Sec. 2)**

1. **§2(1)(A) — "by a single vessel."** The 10,000 mt/yr threshold is measured per vessel, so an operator can divide output across multiple hulls (e.g., one production vessel offloading to several shuttle carriers) and argue no single vessel "recovered" more than the threshold. Fleet structuring defeats the trigger.

2. **§2(1)(A) — "per year."** Undefined: calendar year, fiscal year, rolling 12 months, or 12 months from first recovery? An operator can straddle two calendar years with a 19,999-ton campaign, and enforcers will have no agreed accounting period.

3. **§2(1)(A) — "metric tons."** The bill doesn't say wet weight, dry weight, nodules only, or nodules plus entrained sediment and water. Wet-vs-dry alone can shift reported tonnage by 30–40%, and operators will choose the measure that keeps them under the line.

4. **§2(1)(A) — "recovery."** Undefined. Is a nodule "recovered" when the collector lifts it off the seabed, when it enters the riser, when it reaches the deck, or when it is landed ashore? The point of measurement determines who is liable and when a violation "occurs" for daily penalties under §5(a).

5. **§2(1)(A) — "vessel."** Seabed collectors and ROVs are unmanned vehicles, not vessels in the ordinary maritime sense. An operator can argue the collector (which does the recovering) is not a vessel and the surface ship (which is a vessel) does not "recover from the seabed."

6. **§2(1)(A) — "or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters."** This sweeps in deepwater oil and gas, deepwater sand/aggregate, and OCS hard minerals under Interior's OCSLA authority. The overbreadth guarantees opposition from other industries and invites an argument that Congress could not have meant what the text says, undermining the plain-text reading everywhere else.

7. **§2(1)(B) — "the Secretary."** The term is never defined. Commerce (NOAA), Interior, and State all have plausible claims, so nobody clearly has authority to make the "comparable risk" determination, and any determination is challengeable on that ground alone.

8. **§2(1)(B) — "comparable risks" determination.** No rulemaking procedure, notice-and-comment requirement, evidentiary standard, or judicial review provision. Because the determination defines conduct punishable by 10 years' imprisonment under §5(b), it is exposed to vagueness, due process, and nondelegation challenges, and the rule of lenity will narrow it.

9. **§2(2) — "corporation organized under the laws of a State."** Excludes LLCs, LPs, partnerships, trusts, and other non-corporate entities; excludes entities organized under federal law or the laws of D.C., Puerto Rico, Guam, or other territories; and excludes U.S. nationals and permanent residents. A U.S. mining company reorganized as a Delaware LLC is, by the text, not a "U.S. person."

10. **§2(2) — no control or affiliate test.** Foreign subsidiaries of U.S. corporations, and foreign entities owned or controlled by U.S. persons, are outside the definition. A U.S. parent can place the mining operation in a Cayman or Marshall Islands subsidiary with a foreign-flagged vessel and be outside §3(a) entirely.

11. **§2(3) — "covered vessel" is disconnected from the prohibition.** The 5,000 GT threshold governs only the registry (§4), while the §3 prohibition applies regardless of vessel size. Vessels under 5,000 GT (or operations using several sub-5,000 GT hulls) never register and never report, so the data needed to enforce §3 is never collected.

12. **§2(3) — "equipped for the recovery."** Undefined. A ship that carries a detachable collector, tows a separate collector platform, or is equipped only for lifting/offloading can argue it is not itself "equipped for recovery."

**Prohibition (Sec. 3)**

13. **§3(a) — "any person in the United States."** Mining occurs on the high seas, so a foreign company with U.S. offices will argue it is not "in the United States" when the prohibited act occurs. The phrase's territorial reach is unclear and may add nothing beyond "U.S. person."

14. **§3(a) — "engage in."** Undefined. It is unclear whether owning, chartering, financing, insuring, directing, crewing, or contracting for mining counts. There is no "cause," "aid or abet," "attempt," or "conspire" language, so U.S. capital, management, and offtake can support a foreign-conducted operation without clearly violating the Act.

15. **§3(a) — no import, landing, processing, or transshipment ban.** Nodules mined by a foreign operator can be landed, processed, refined, and sold in the United States with no restriction. The Act stops U.S. operators, not the U.S. market, which is the economic driver.

16. **§3(b) — exploration license exemption is the core loophole.** It exempts "mining conducted under an exploration license," but exploration licenses (e.g., under DSHMRA) do not authorize commercial recovery, so the clause either exempts nothing or exempts everything an existing licensee chooses to do. Read naturally, any holder of a pre-enactment exploration license is grandfathered for all mining, of any scale, indefinitely.

17. **§3(b) — "issued" by whom, and when.** The clause does not say the license must be issued by the United States, so ISA exploration contracts sponsored by foreign states arguably qualify. It also does not address licenses amended, renewed, extended, transferred, or converted to recovery permits after enactment, each of which an operator will argue remains the "license issued before" enactment.

18. **§3(b) — no duration or scope limit.** The grandfather has no end date, no tonnage cap, and no geographic tie to the licensed area. Combined with the 10-year sunset in §7(b), an existing licensee can operate continuously through the life of the Act.

19. **§3(c) — "for the purpose of environmental assessment."** No definition, no tonnage cap, no permit, no approving agency, and a purely subjective purpose test. Pilot collection and test mining can be characterized as environmental assessment; mixed-purpose activities (assess *and* sell the nodules) are unaddressed.

20. **§3 — no exemption for scientific research, cable/pipeline work, salvage, or dredging.** Given the breadth of §2(1)(A), these activities at depth are technically covered. Overbreadth invites as-applied challenges and undercuts the statute's credibility in court.

21. **§3 — no U.S. waters carve-out or conflict provision.** The prohibition applies to the U.S. continental shelf and EEZ at depths over 200 m, overlapping Interior's OCSLA authority, without amending or reconciling that statute.

22. **§3 — DSHMRA is left intact.** The Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act (30 U.S.C. 1401 et seq.) still authorizes NOAA to issue exploration licenses and commercial recovery permits. Two unreconciled statutes create implied-repeal litigation and leave NOAA able to issue new licenses during the 180-day pre-effective window.

**Registry (Sec. 4)**

23. **§4(a) — no deadline, content, or scope.** The registration requirement has no due date, no required information, no fee, and does not say whether it applies to U.S.-flagged vessels, vessels of U.S. operators, or every covered vessel worldwide. As to foreign vessels it is unenforceable; as to domestic ones it is undefined.

24. **§4(a)–(b) — "operator" undefined.** Owner, charterer, manager, or master? Without a definition, the obligation can be shuffled among entities so that none is clearly responsible.

25. **§4(b) — reports don't require tonnage.** Reports need only "describe" recovery activities, not quantify them. The one data point needed to enforce the 10,000 mt threshold is not mandated.

26. **§4 — no penalty, verification, or inspection authority.** Section 5 penalizes only §3 violations, so failure to register or filing a false report carries no penalty under this Act. There is no inspection, boarding, audit, recordkeeping, observer, AIS, or subpoena authority, and "certified by the operator" is not tied to penalty of perjury.

**Penalties (Sec. 5)**

27. **§5(a) vs. §8 — penalty date conflicts with effective date.** Penalties attach to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but §3 is not effective until 180 days later. Conduct in that window cannot be a "violation" of a provision not yet in effect, and the language invites retroactivity and due-process challenges.

28. **§5(a) — "each day on which the violation occurs" mismatched with an annual threshold.** The offense is defined by cumulative annual tonnage, so it is unclear whether a violation "occurs" on the day the 10,001st ton is recovered, every day thereafter, or every day of the year. Defendants will argue one violation per year, capping exposure at $1 million.

29. **§5(a) — no enforcement mechanism.** No agency is designated to assess or collect penalties, no administrative or judicial procedure is specified, and there is no injunctive relief, vessel or cargo forfeiture, permit revocation, debarment, or citizen-suit provision.

30. **§5(b) — "willfully."** The heightened mens rea, layered on undefined terms and a Secretary-made definition, makes criminal prosecution very difficult. A good-faith interpretation of "recovery," "per year," or "environmental assessment" defeats willfulness.

31. **§5 — no individual or officer liability and no entity-attribution rule.** Nothing addresses liability of directors, officers, or parent companies, or attribution of a vessel's conduct to its owner, so liability can be isolated in a judgment-proof single-vessel entity.

**International Agreement (Sec. 6)**

32. **§6 — hortatory and ambiguous timing.** "Shall seek to negotiate" imposes no obligation to conclude anything and has no reporting or consequence. "Not later than 18 months" is ambiguous as to whether it governs when negotiations begin or when an agreement is reached.

**Duration (Sec. 7)**

33. **§7(a) — no mechanism for the NAS report.** No one is directed or funded to commission the National Academies study, and "serious harm" is undefined. The lifting condition can never be triggered as drafted, so the only operative exit is the sunset.

34. **§7(a) vs. §7(b) — internal tension.** Subsection (a) says the prohibition lasts until Congress finds mining safe; subsection (b) ends the entire Act after 10 years regardless. Opponents of the bill will read (b) as controlling, and the result is an automatic lapse with no findings required.

35. **§7(b) — "this Act shall cease to have effect."** Because the whole Act, including §5, expires, pending enforcement actions and prosecutions may abate. Whether the general savings statute (1 U.S.C. 109) applies to an Act that "ceases to have effect" rather than one that is "repealed" is unsettled, and late-period violations become practically unpunishable.

36. **§7(b) and §8 — dates keyed inconsistently.** The sunset runs from enactment while the prohibition starts 180 days later, so the operative ban is 9.5 years. Enactment, effective date, grandfather date, and penalty date are four different reference points across §§3(b), 5(a), 7(b), and 8.

**Effective Date and General Provisions**

37. **§8 — 180-day window.** Operators can accelerate recovery, stockpile, and secure or amend exploration licenses before the prohibition takes effect. Licenses issued in this window are not grandfathered under §3(b) but the conduct is not yet unlawful, creating an odd gap.

38. **No severability clause.** If §2(1)(B), the extraterritorial reach of §3(a), or the overbroad "other mineral resources" language is struck, a court may invalidate the entire Act.

39. **No rulemaking authority or authorization of appropriations.** NOAA is given a registry to run with no implementing authority, no funding, and no deadline for standing it up.

40. **No savings or preemption clause.** The Act does not address state law, existing contracts, pending NOAA proceedings, or treaty obligations, leaving all of those to litigation.

41. **Takings exposure.** Holders of DSHMRA licenses and permits who are *not* covered by §3(b) (e.g., those whose licenses are reissued, renewed, or converted after enactment) have invested in reliance on federal authorization, and the Act contains no compensation or reliance provision, inviting Fifth Amendment claims.

---

**Most consequential for the markup:** items 1, 9–10, 16–19, 27–28, and 34–35. The exploration-license grandfather (§3(b)) and the environmental-assessment exemption (§3(c)) together arguably exempt most existing or planned U.S. operations outright; the "U.S. person" definition (§2(2)) can be avoided by entity restructuring; and the penalty/effective-date conflicts plus the hard sunset substantially weaken enforcement.
